narrative:
The model determined that you have a 93% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants to admit students likely to succeed, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

Three aspects of your academic record were especially influential in this decision. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the single biggest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. While accepted students typically rank around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom 20%, which strongly signaled future difficulty passing the bar. Your LSAT score was the second most important driver; at 28 it sits well below the average of 37 among admitted students, further increasing the model’s concern about your readiness. Your first-year class ranking came third. Like your third-year rank, it was also in the bottom 20%, again pulling the prediction away from success.

Taken together, these three academic signals outweighed other information such as your solid undergraduate GPA of 3.6, your middle-income background, and your plan to attend full-time. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT. Raising either your class standing or your test score would likely shift future predictions in your favor. You may want to speak with an admissions counselor about targeted academic support programs before reapplying.
